meta.blurb: Catherine Morland has read so many ghost stories that she expects a secret behind every door. At Northanger Abbey she finds a black cabinet in her room and a host whose wife died years ago. She is sure there is a crime.
meta.bible: Catherine Morland: the heroine, seventeen, a clergyman's daughter from Fullerton; open-hearted, honest and in love with Gothic novels. Mr Morland and Mrs Morland: her parents, kind and sensible; one of ten children. James Morland: her elder brother, a student at Oxford. Mr Allen and Mrs Allen: rich, childless neighbours who take Catherine to Bath; Mr Allen is calm, Mrs Allen thinks only of clothes. Isabella Thorpe: pretty, lively and falsely warm; Catherine's new friend. Mrs Thorpe: her mother, an old school friend of Mrs Allen. John Thorpe: Isabella's brother, loud, boastful and a liar. Henry Tilney: a witty young clergyman of about twenty-six; he lives at Woodston parsonage. Eleanor Tilney: his gentle sister. Captain Frederick Tilney: their elder brother, a handsome army officer. General Tilney: their stern, proud father, owner of Northanger Abbey; obsessed with money and comfort. Mrs Tilney: the General's wife, who died nine years before. Places: Fullerton, Catherine's village; Bath, the fashionable town with its Pump Room, Upper Rooms and Beechen Cliff; Northanger Abbey, an old house in Gloucestershire made modern inside; Woodston, Henry's village; Oxford; Clifton. Fixed facts: the Gothic novel Catherine loves is The Mysteries of Udolpho by Mrs Radcliffe; the black cabinet and old chest in her bedroom hold only a laundry list; the General sends her home in a coach without a servant. Voice and tone: light, funny and teasing; the narrator laughs gently at Catherine and at novels, and ends on a smile.

B1B2: Catherine Morland was one of ten children, and nobody expected her to become a heroine. She preferred cricket and rolling down the green hill to dolls, and she loved to be outdoors all day.
By the age of seventeen, Catherine had grown pretty and sweet, and she had begun to read novels. She liked the frightening ones best, with dark castles and secret rooms, and she believed every word.
Mr and Mrs Allen, rich neighbours who had no children, were going to Bath for the winter. They asked Catherine to come with them, and her parents agreed, so she packed with great joy.

The journey was pleasant, and Catherine looked out of the window at every hill and village. When they reached Bath, the tall stone houses and busy streets seemed to her the most wonderful sight in the world.
On their first evening, the Allens took Catherine to a ball in the Upper Rooms. The room was so crowded that she could hardly move, and as she knew nobody, she had to sit and watch.
At last, the master of ceremonies introduced Catherine to a young man named Henry Tilney. He was handsome and lively, and they danced together, and she enjoyed every moment of it.

Henry teased Catherine about the diary that every girl in Bath was supposed to keep. He also joked, with a straight face, about what a fashionable gown might cost, and Catherine laughed and liked him.
Mrs Allen met an old school friend, Mrs Thorpe, who had a lively, pretty daughter named Isabella. Isabella was a few years older than Catherine, and she soon treated her like a dear friend.

Catherine and Isabella spent whole mornings reading a frightening novel called The Mysteries of Udolpho. They talked about the story, told each other their secrets and promised to be best friends for ever.

To Catherine's delight, her brother James arrived from Oxford, bringing his friend John Thorpe, who was Isabella's brother. John was loud and rude, and he talked constantly about his horses, his carriage and himself.
James and Isabella grew fonder of each other every day, and Catherine was delighted for them both. She hoped to see Henry Tilney again, but he and his sister seemed to have left Bath.
At the theatre, Catherine saw Henry Tilney again, and she was delighted. He introduced her to his sister Eleanor, a quiet, kind girl, and they agreed to take a walk together the next morning.
On the morning of the walk, it rained, and Catherine had to wait indoors. When the weather cleared, the Thorpes arrived in their carriage and insisted that Catherine should come with them to Clifton.
As the carriage drove through the town, Catherine saw Henry and Eleanor walking in the street. She asked John to stop, but he only laughed and drove faster, and she realised that he had lied.
The next day, Catherine hurried to the Tilneys' lodgings to explain what had happened. Eleanor listened kindly and forgave her at once, and their father, General Tilney, was polite and welcoming.
On the walk to Beechen Cliff, Catherine and Henry spoke about books, history and novels. He laughed at her love of frightening stories, but he liked her all the more for being so honest.
James told Catherine that Isabella had agreed to marry him, and Catherine was thrilled. His father gave his consent, but the family had little money, and Isabella said she did not mind at all.
James rode home to arrange the engagement with his parents, and Isabella waited for his return. She quickly grew bored without him, and she began to look at other young men with interest.
Henry's brother, Captain Frederick Tilney, came to Bath for a visit. He was handsome, confident and a soldier, and Isabella soon paid him a great deal of attention.

Catherine told Henry that she was worried about her brother, and that Isabella was behaving strangely. Henry said, with a sigh, that his brother was fond of flirting but would probably do no real harm.
Before they left Bath, General Tilney asked Catherine to visit his home, Northanger Abbey. Catherine had never been so excited, and her friends agreed that she should go.

On the journey, Henry teased Catherine with a long, funny story of the terrible things she might find at the Abbey. He told her about secret rooms, sliding panels and a storm that would shake the old walls.

To Catherine's surprise, the Abbey was warm and bright, with large windows and modern fireplaces. General Tilney was very proud of his improvements, and he showed her every room, including the new kitchen.
In her bedroom, Catherine found a big old chest and a black cabinet. During a storm that night, she opened the cabinet, found a roll of paper inside, and hoped it was a secret.

In the morning light, Catherine looked at the roll of papers again and discovered that it was nothing but a list of washing. She felt very silly, and she hid it under the bed so that nobody would know.

General Tilney walked Catherine through the gardens and the greenhouses. He spoke of his late wife, Mrs Tilney, who had died nine years before, and Catherine thought that his voice had a strange sound.
Catherine remembered all her novels, and she decided that General Tilney must have been cruel to his wife. She thought he might even have locked her away, or worse, and she watched him with fear.
One afternoon, Catherine crept down a long corridor to the room where Mrs Tilney had died. She was sure that she would find proof of a terrible crime, and her hands were cold with fear.
The room was large, light and quite ordinary, with a bed and a window looking over the garden. As she turned to leave, Catherine saw Henry coming toward her, and she was very afraid.

Henry told her gravely that her suspicions about his father were dreadful and quite untrue. He asked her to think about the world she lived in, and to remember that people in England do not usually commit murders.
Catherine ran to her room and cried with shame. Later, Henry spoke to her kindly, and she decided that she would never again let novels fool her about real life.
A few days later, Catherine received a letter from James. He told her that Isabella had ended their engagement, and that she was now in love with Captain Frederick Tilney.
Catherine told Henry and Eleanor about the broken engagement, and they were sorry for James. Henry said he doubted that his brother really loved Isabella, and Eleanor was ashamed of him.
A letter arrived from Isabella, full of sweet words and warm wishes, as if nothing had happened. She wanted Catherine to speak to James and tell him that she had always loved only him.
Henry went to his home in Woodston for a few days, to see to his parish. Catherine and Eleanor stayed together at the Abbey, and they were very happy, especially when the General was away.
General Tilney took Catherine and Eleanor to Woodston, to see Henry's home. Catherine thought the house was charming, and the General made hints that she might one day live there.
One day, General Tilney came home suddenly from London, in a bad mood. He spoke sharply to Eleanor, and the family seemed to be afraid of him.
That evening, Eleanor came to Catherine's room in tears and said that her father wanted Catherine to leave early the next morning. She could not say why, and she was deeply ashamed.
At seven in the morning, Catherine said goodbye to Eleanor, who was in tears, and left the Abbey. She had no servant, and she had to travel seventy miles alone in a common coach.
Catherine arrived home late in the day, tired, hungry and very unhappy. Her family was astonished to see her, and she burst into tears as soon as she saw her mother.
Mrs Morland said that General Tilney had behaved very rudely, and that Catherine should try not to think about him. But Catherine could not forget Henry, and she grew quiet and sad.
A few days later, Henry arrived at the Morland house, hot and tired from his long ride. He seemed shy and uneasy, and the Morlands wondered what he wanted.

Henry explained the whole matter to Catherine and her parents. General Tilney had believed that Catherine was rich, because John Thorpe had boasted about her family, and he had wanted her to marry his son.
Later, John Thorpe was angry because Catherine would not accept his attentions, and he told the General that the Morlands were poor. The General, who cared above all for money, sent her away at once.
Henry said that he was ashamed of his father's behaviour and that he would not obey him in this. He asked Catherine to marry him, and she said yes, very happily.
Mr and Mrs Morland liked Henry very much and were happy for their daughter. But they said that they could not agree to the wedding until General Tilney had given his full consent.

While Henry and Catherine waited, Eleanor married a rich man of high rank, and this made her father very happy. For a time, the General was so pleased with the news that he hardly thought of anything else.
The General discovered, to his relief, that the Morlands were a comfortable and respectable family. Catherine would have a small fortune, and he realised that he had made a foolish mistake.
At last, after many weeks, General Tilney sent his consent by letter. He did not do it warmly or with a good grace, but he did not refuse, and the young couple were free to marry.
Catherine and Henry were married in the village church, with her whole family present. They were happy, and the story ends with the hope that no one will think that its lesson is anything but kind.
C1C2: Catherine Morland was one of ten children in a clergyman's house, and nobody who knew her as a child would have guessed that she was born to be a heroine. She cared nothing for dolls and gardens, preferring cricket, riding and rolling down the green hill behind the house, and she was far more at home in mud than in manners. Nothing in her early life, in short, gave the slightest hint of anything romantic, and her family certainly expected none.

By seventeen she had grown into a pleasant-looking girl with a warm heart and a rather simple mind, and she had developed a taste for novels. She liked the frightening ones best, full of dark castles, secret passages and wicked villains, and she believed, without stopping to doubt, that real life must be much the same. It was a harmless enough belief in itself, but it would cost her a number of blushes before the year was over.

Mr and Mrs Allen, a wealthy neighbouring couple who had no children of their own, were going to spend the winter in Bath for the sake of Mr Allen's health. They kindly invited Catherine to go with them, and her parents, who saw no reason to refuse, gave their consent. She packed her bags with a joy that no history of Bath could have dimmed.

The journey passed without adventure, though Catherine looked out of the window at every hill and village as if each one might hide a mystery. When they reached Bath, with its tall pale houses, its crowded streets and its air of constant celebration, she thought she had arrived in the most wonderful town in the world. Even Mrs Allen, who had seen the town many times before and thought little of it, shared a small part of her young friend's wonder.

On their first evening, Mrs Allen took Catherine to a ball in the Upper Rooms, where the crowd was so dense that they could hardly move without being pushed. Mrs Allen knew no one there, and neither did Catherine, so they spent the night looking at the dancers and wishing that someone would speak to them. It was not at all the glittering beginning that she had imagined on the long road, and she went to bed a little sad.

At last the master of ceremonies, who had noticed her sitting alone, introduced Catherine to a young gentleman named Henry Tilney. He was handsome, amusing and not at all shy, and she found herself dancing with him and laughing, which was exactly what she had come to Bath for. By the end of the dance she had decided that this was the first truly pleasant evening of her whole stay in the town.

Henry teased her gently about the diary that he supposed she kept of every day in Bath, and he pretended to know a great deal about the price of fashionable muslin. Catherine was not accustomed to being talked to in this playful way, and she was half amused and half bewildered, but she decided, almost at once, that she liked him very much. Unfortunately, although she looked for him eagerly in every room, he was nowhere to be seen on the following day.

Mrs Allen chanced to meet an old school friend, Mrs Thorpe, and the two ladies settled down to a long comparison of their children and their husbands. Mrs Thorpe's eldest daughter, Isabella, was a lively, fashionable girl a few years older than Catherine, and within a few minutes she was treating her new acquaintance as a friend of long standing. Catherine, who had been so lonely, was flattered and relieved, and she could hardly believe her good luck.

The two girls spent whole mornings together reading The Mysteries of Udolpho, a novel by Mrs Radcliffe that Catherine thought the most thrilling book ever written. They discussed the story as though it were real, exchanged confidences about their hopes and promised each other a friendship that would last for ever. Isabella's promises were very large indeed, and, as Catherine would one day learn, they came to her much too easily.

To Catherine's great delight, her brother James arrived from Oxford with a friend, who proved to be none other than John Thorpe, Isabella's brother. John was a noisy, conceited young man who talked constantly about his horses, his carriage and his own cleverness, and Catherine soon decided that she did not like him. Unfortunately for her peace, he seemed to have decided in the first five minutes that he liked her extremely.

It was soon plain to everyone that James and Isabella were falling in love, and Catherine, who adored them both, was delighted at the thought of becoming her friend's sister. She was less happy on her own account, for she searched the Pump Room and the ballroom in vain for Henry Tilney, who seemed to have disappeared. She found it hard to enjoy any party or any walk without him, and she was annoyed to find it so.

To her great relief, Catherine saw Henry Tilney at the theatre, and he came across the room to speak to her at once. He introduced her to his sister Eleanor, a gentle and graceful girl, and they arranged to take a walk together the next morning if the weather permitted. Catherine, who had been lonely and anxious for days, went home in the best of spirits.

On the morning of the planned walk, it rained, and Catherine waited anxiously at the window in case the weather should clear. When it did, the Thorpes and James appeared in a carriage and begged her to join them on an outing to Clifton, and John added that he had seen the Tilneys driving out of town. Catherine, who did not want to doubt a friend's brother, reluctantly agreed to go, though her heart was far from willing.

As they drove through the town, Catherine saw Henry and Eleanor Tilney walking quietly along the pavement, exactly where John had said they would not be. She cried out and begged him to stop the carriage, but he only laughed and whipped up the horse, and she understood, with horror and shame, that he had lied to her. The drive to Clifton, which was supposed to be an hour of fun, was for her a long and very silent one.

The very next morning, Catherine hurried to the Tilneys' lodgings to explain how she had been carried off, and her words came out in a rush of apology. Eleanor forgave her at once, her brother Henry smiled, and their father, General Tilney, who had a stiff, handsome manner, received her with every mark of kindness. Her anxiety melted away like morning frost, and she left the house in a glow of relief and gratitude.

On the walk up Beechen Cliff, Catherine and Henry talked about history, novels and everything in between, and he showed himself to be better read than she had expected. He teased her about her love of frightening stories, yet he did not despise her for it, and Catherine found that she did not mind being laughed at by someone so clearly kind. The afternoon, with its views, its books and its laughter, was one of the happiest of her whole stay in Bath.

James announced that Isabella had agreed to marry him, and Catherine, who loved them both, was overjoyed at the prospect of such a sister. Mr Morland gave his consent, but the family could not afford to give very much, and Isabella declared with a charming smile that she cared nothing for money. Catherine, who believed her without question, thought it the most generous speech that she had ever heard from anyone.

James rode home to arrange the engagement with his parents, and Isabella, left behind in Bath with nothing to do, grew restless and bored. She declared that she missed him dreadfully, but she was seen more and more often at the side of other young men, and Catherine, watching, felt the first faint stirrings of doubt. She told herself firmly that she must be mistaken, because she could not believe so dear a friend capable of unkindness.

Henry's elder brother, Captain Frederick Tilney, arrived in Bath with the confident air of a handsome soldier who knows his own worth. Isabella, who had promised herself to James, took one look at him and began to flirt, and the Captain, who was no fool, was not slow to flirt back. Catherine, who still believed in the natural goodness of everyone she met, was shocked, and she did not know where to look.

Catherine confided to Henry that she was uneasy about her brother and about the way Isabella was behaving with the Captain. Henry, who knew his brother better than he wished to, admitted with a sigh that Frederick was fond of flirting, though he hoped it would come to nothing. His honesty comforted her a great deal, though it did not quite satisfy her, and she went on watching her brother's face.

As the winter drew to a close, General Tilney, who had taken a great liking to Catherine, invited her to stay for some weeks at Northanger Abbey, the family's home. Catherine, who had read of old abbeys in a dozen novels and had dreamed of living in one, accepted at once, and the Allens saw no reason to refuse. She could hardly wait to see it with her own eyes, and she lay awake for hours that night imagining its towers and its dark stairs.

As they drove through the dusk, Henry amused himself by describing the horrors that might await her at Northanger Abbey, with its secret passages, sliding panels and a lost manuscript hidden in a chest. Catherine listened with wide eyes, half afraid and half delighted, and she did not notice that he was laughing. By the time the carriage arrived at the great gate, she was ready for any horror that the old walls could offer.

To her surprise and a little to her disappointment, Northanger Abbey proved to be warm, light and thoroughly comfortable, with large windows, modern stoves and not a single secret passage in sight. General Tilney, who had spent much money on his improvements, was proud of every one of them and took great pains to show her the new kitchen and the gardens. It was all very different from the gloomy castle of Udolpho, and she tried hard not to feel cheated.

In her bedchamber she found a large old chest and a tall black cabinet, and in her excited state she was sure that they held some great secret. That night a storm broke over the Abbey, and by the light of a single candle she searched the cabinet and found a roll of papers hidden at the back. She had only just begun to make out the first words, in a faded hand, when the candle suddenly went out and left her in the dark.

In the light of morning, Catherine unrolled the mysterious papers and found, in a clear and ordinary hand, nothing more thrilling than a washing list, including shirts, stockings and a few pocket handkerchiefs. She blushed deeply at her own foolishness and hid the paper before anyone could see it, but she could not entirely forget how very frightened she had been. It was a lesson she would need to repeat before she finally learned it, and the next one came sooner than she could have guessed.

General Tilney showed her his gardens, his greenhouses and every corner of his proud estate, and from time to time he mentioned his late wife, Mrs Tilney, who had died nine years before. Catherine noticed that Eleanor grew silent whenever her mother was mentioned, and that the General's voice took on a cold and stiff tone. Her imagination, which was never idle for long in the presence of a mystery, began at once to work upon these small and innocent hints.

Remembering every wicked husband she had ever met in a novel, Catherine decided that General Tilney had been cruel to his wife, and that her death had not been quite what the family said. She imagined that Mrs Tilney might still be locked in some secret room, or that she had been killed in some terrible way, and she watched the General with growing fear. Nothing the poor man did, from carving the meat to opening a door, could be entirely innocent in her eyes any longer.

One afternoon, when she believed herself unobserved, Catherine crept down a long corridor towards the rooms where Mrs Tilney had died, her heart beating hard and her hands cold. She was determined to find some trace of a terrible crime, some dark stain or some hidden sign, and she opened the door with a trembling hand. What she saw, when the door swung open, was only a bright, pleasant and entirely ordinary room that anyone might be glad to sleep in.

The room was large, light and cheerful, with a fine bed, a pleasant window and nothing in it more sinister than a vase of flowers. As she stood there feeling foolish, she heard footsteps on the stairs, and Henry appeared in the doorway, looking at her with an expression she had not seen before. She understood at once, with a rush of shame, that he had somehow guessed every thought that had been in her head.

Henry told her, with a gravity that stung more than anger would have done, that her suspicions about his father were dreadful and entirely without foundation. He asked her to consider the country she lived in, the age they were born into and the laws and newspapers that watched over every neighbour, and to ask herself whether such horrors were likely. Catherine, in tears, saw the whole truth at once, and she was more ashamed than she had ever been in her life.

Catherine fled to her room and wept with shame, certain that Henry would never speak to her again. At dinner, however, he treated her with perfect kindness and not a word of reproach, and she resolved, with a deep sense of gratitude, that she would never again let a novel govern her judgement of living people. It was a lesson she felt deep within herself, and it changed the way she looked at the world for the rest of her days.

A few days later, a letter arrived from James, written in a hand that shook with misery, telling Catherine that Isabella had broken their engagement. Isabella, it seemed, had been more taken with the Captain than with the poor student, and had thrown James over without any hesitation or regret. Catherine read it three times over, in the bright morning light, before she could make herself believe a single word of it.

Catherine told Henry and Eleanor about the broken engagement, trembling a little, for she half expected them to defend their brother. To her relief they were sincerely sorry, and Eleanor was ashamed of him, while Henry, after a thoughtful pause, said that he doubted whether the Captain truly cared for Isabella at all. They did not make any excuses for him, and Catherine loved them more for their plain and honest way of speaking.

Soon afterwards, Isabella herself wrote a long letter full of sweet words and warm affection, as if nothing whatever had come between them. She hinted that the Captain had treated her badly, and begged Catherine to speak for her to James, assuring her that she had always loved him alone. Catherine read it twice and saw her false friend clearly for the first time, and she was surprised at how little it hurt her.

Henry rode off to his parish at Woodston to attend to his duties, and for a few days Catherine and Eleanor had the Abbey almost to themselves. The General himself was away from home for part of the time, and the two girls, relieved of his watchful eye, talked, walked and read together with an ease that Catherine had not known before. It was a short season of perfect peace, and she remembered it long afterwards as one of the sweetest of her life.

The General drove Catherine and Eleanor over to Woodston to see Henry's parsonage, a small and cheerful house with a pretty garden and a comfortable parlour. He praised every detail of it, asked her opinion more than once and made several remarks that Catherine, who was not quick, took to be mere politeness. Henry, who was present and understood exactly what his father meant, grew a little red in the face and looked away.

One day, after a short absence in London, General Tilney returned unexpectedly, in a thoroughly bad temper, and the whole house seemed to tighten with fear. He spoke sharply to Eleanor, would not meet Catherine's eyes and sat through dinner in a thundery silence, and neither of the girls could think what they had done to offend him. Catherine, for once, did not suspect a murder, but she felt that something very unpleasant was surely about to happen.

That evening Eleanor came to Catherine's room in tears and told her, with a trembling voice, that her father required her to leave early the next morning. She could give no reason, apologised again and again and was plainly ashamed of the rudeness of the order, which sent a guest away without a servant and without any explanation. Catherine, who was stunned by the unfairness of it, could only ask what she had done to deserve such treatment.

At seven the next morning, Catherine said a sad goodbye to the weeping Eleanor and was driven away from the Abbey in a hired coach, with no servant to guard her and no friend to comfort her. She was obliged to make a journey of about seventy miles alone, which was thought very improper for a young woman, and which the General seemed not to mind at all. She was too unhappy to be frightened, and she watched the grey fields go by without seeing a single one of them.

Late in the afternoon, Catherine arrived at her father's door, tired, hungry and heartsick, and her astonished family could hardly believe their eyes. She burst into tears at the sight of her mother, told her story as best she could, and was rather comforted than not to find that nobody blamed her for anything. Home, she thought, as she wiped her face, was after all the very best place in the world in which to be miserable.

Mrs Morland, a calm and sensible woman, said that General Tilney had undoubtedly behaved very badly, and that Catherine would do well to put the whole affair out of her mind and attend to her mending. Catherine tried to obey, but her thoughts continually returned to Henry and to the possibility that she would never see him again, and in a week or so she grew pale and silent. Her family, who had never seen her so quiet, began to worry about her and to speak of it in low voices.

A few days later, Henry rode up to the Morland house, rather dusty from his long journey and a little uneasy about what he had come to say. He had ridden a long way, in direct defiance of his father's wishes, and he was not at all sure of his welcome, though Catherine's face, when she saw him, left him in no doubt. The Morlands, who were mystified by his visit and a little alarmed by it, offered him tea and waited patiently to hear his business.

Henry explained everything with perfect frankness, though he was visibly ashamed of his father. The General had been told by John Thorpe, in one of his boastful moods, that the Morlands were extremely wealthy, and had therefore been anxious to win Catherine for his son. Catherine could hardly believe that anyone could be moved by such a motive, or that John Thorpe was the cause of all her trouble.

Later, when Catherine had refused to encourage his own attentions, Thorpe turned spiteful and told the General, with equal confidence, that the Morlands were not wealthy at all. The General, who valued money above everything and was furious at having been so deceived, hurried home and ordered the girl out of his house with a rudeness that his children could hardly forgive. It was a cruel, vulgar and very petty reason for treating a young girl so badly, and Catherine thought so too.

Henry declared that he was thoroughly ashamed of his father's conduct and that he would no longer be ruled by him in a matter of the heart, since he had decided that he would marry Catherine whatever happened. He asked her gently whether she would accept him, and she, who had hardly dared to hope for such a thing, accepted without a moment's hesitation. They were both very happy and also rather tearful, and the Morlands, who stood by, were charmed with them.

Mr and Mrs Morland liked Henry extremely and were glad to see their daughter so well suited, but they were sensible people and said that they could not allow the engagement to proceed without General Tilney's full consent. Henry, though disappointed, saw that this was fair, and he returned to Woodston to wait, while Catherine, who had no wish to rush, settled down to wait with him. It was a long wait, but they bore it with the patience of two people who were quite certain of each other.

While the lovers waited, Eleanor was fortunate enough to marry a gentleman of rank, wealth and excellent character, and the General, delighted with the match, was in the best of humours for months together. Nobody dared to remind him of the young couple at Woodston, and nobody needed to, for his temper, for once, was kind. Henry, who was a patient man, took the opportunity to write a polite and careful letter to his father about Catherine.

Around the same time, the General discovered, to his considerable relief, that the Morlands were a comfortable and respectable family, and that Catherine would receive a small but decent fortune. He had, it appeared, been deceived in both directions, and the knowledge that his anger had been built on a lie did something to soften him. He began, by slow degrees, to look at the match with a more forgiving eye, and to wonder what he had been so angry about.

At last, after months of delay, General Tilney sent his consent, not warmly or with any grace, but plainly and without further objection. Henry and Catherine, who had waited long enough, thought it the most beautiful consent that had ever been written, and they did not trouble themselves about the manner of its giving. Everything else was easy after that, and the young people were surprised at how quickly the long storm blew away.

Catherine and Henry were married in the little church at Fullerton, with her whole large family present and the General, at a distance, doing his best to look pleased. They began their life together with love, good sense and a small, comfortable fortune, and the author hopes, with a smile, that no reader will think that a story of persecution ends in anything but a happy marriage. It is a story, after all, about a girl who learned to see the world as it truly is, and who was happy to find it kinder than the books had promised.
